claims.interpretation: The paper identifies a lack of a framework to organize existing language agents and plan future developments, motivating the proposal of CoALA.
The paper proposes Cognitive Architectures for Language Agents (CoALA), drawing on cognitive science and symbolic AI.
CoALA describes a language agent with modular memory components, a structured action space for internal memory and external environments, and a generalized decision-making process.
CoALA is used to retrospectively survey and organize recent work and prospectively identify actionable directions for more capable agents.
CoALA contextualizes language agents within the broader history of AI and outlines a path towards language-based general intelligence.
Language agents are an emerging class of AI systems that use large language models to interact with the world.
Language agents apply advances in LLMs to the existing field of agent design, benefiting both fields.
LLMs have limited knowledge and reasoning capabilities, which language agents mitigate by connecting LLMs to external resources.
Language agents leverage commonsense priors in LLMs to adapt to novel tasks, reducing dependence on human annotation or trial-and-error learning.
Traditional agents often require handcrafted rules or reinforcement learning, making generalization to new environments challenging.
Earliest language agents used LLMs to directly select or generate actions, while more recent agents use them for reasoning, planning, and long-term memory management.
Individual works use custom terminology for internal processes, making it difficult to compare agents, understand evolution, or build new agents with clean abstractions.
The paper draws a parallel between production systems and LLMs, suggesting that cognitive architecture controls used with production systems may be applicable to transform LLMs into language agents.
The paper proposes a conceptual framework organizing efforts by drawing parallels with production systems and cognitive architectures from the history of computing and AI.
The paper proposes Cognitive Architectures for Language Agents (CoALA), a conceptual framework to characterize and design general purpose language agents.

CoALA organizes agents along three key dimensions: information storage (working and long-term memories), action space (internal and external actions), and decision-making procedure (interactive loop with planning and execution).
CoALA can neatly express a large body of existing agents and identify underexplored directions to develop new ones.
The paper proposes a theoretical framework (CoALA) and uses it to organize diverse empirical work on language agents, grounding theory in existing practices.
The paper identifies both short-term and long-term directions for future work by combining conceptual architecture proposals with empirical surveys.
The paper introduces production systems and cognitive architectures, then shows how recent LLM and language agent developments recapitulate these historical ideas.
The CoALA framework is introduced in Section 4 and used to survey existing language agents.
The paper provides a deeper case study of several prominent agents in Section 5.
Section 6 suggests actionable steps to construct future language agents, and Section 7 highlights open questions in cognitive science and AI.
LLMs are constrained by limited context windows, hindering utility in extended conversations and document analysis.

The paper proposes virtual context management, a technique inspired by hierarchical memory systems in operating systems that provide extended virtual memory via paging between physical memory and disk.
MemGPT is introduced as a system that intelligently manages different storage tiers to effectively provide extended context within the LLM's limited context window.
MemGPT is evaluated in document analysis, where it can analyze large documents exceeding the LLM's context window.
MemGPT is evaluated in multi-session chat, creating agents that remember, reflect, and evolve through long-term interactions.
The limited fixed-length context windows of LLMs significantly hinder their applicability to long conversations or reasoning about long documents.
Most widely used open-source LLMs can only support a few dozen back-and-forth messages or reason about a short document before exceeding their max context window.
Directly extending transformer context length causes quadratic increases in computational time and memory cost due to self-attention.
Long-context models struggle to effectively utilize additional context even if computational challenges are overcome.
There is a critical need for alternative techniques to support long context due to high training costs and diminishing returns of context scaling.
The paper proposes providing the illusion of infinite context while using fixed-context models, borrowing from virtual memory paging.
MemGPT is an OS-inspired LLM system for virtual context management, built on recent progress in function calling abilities of LLM agents.
MemGPT uses function calls to let LLM agents read/write external data sources, modify their own context, and decide when to respond to the user.
MemGPT enables LLMs to page information between context windows (main memory) and external storage, analogous to hierarchical memory in traditional OSes.
Function calls manage control flow among context management, response generation, and user interactions, allowing iterative context modification for a single task.
MemGPT treats context windows as a constrained memory resource and designs a memory hierarchy for LLMs analogous to memory tiers in traditional OSes.
The excerpt does not state limitations or future directions of MemGPT itself; no explicit gap is reported.

claims.interpretation: MemGPT is an LLM OS that lets the LLM manage its own context, analogous to physical memory, to create an illusion of longer context length.
MemGPT enables retrieval of relevant historical data missing from context and eviction of less relevant data to external storage.
The combination of memory-hierarchy, OS functions, and event-based control flow allows MemGPT to handle unbounded context with finite-context LLMs.
MemGPT is evaluated on document analysis and conversational agents, domains where existing LLMs are limited by finite context.
MemGPT overcomes finite context limitations to outperform existing LLM-based approaches in both tested settings.
MemGPT augments a fixed-context LLM processor with a hierarchical memory system and functions for self-managing memory.
MemGPT's main context consists of system instructions, working context, and a FIFO queue; outputs are interpreted as function calls.
MemGPT uses functions to move data between main context and external context (archival and recall storage databases).
MemGPT enables function chaining via a request_heartbeat=true keyword argument, allowing multi-step retrieval to answer user queries.
LongMemEval is a benchmark evaluating five core long-term memory abilities of chat assistants: information extraction, multi-session reasoning, temporal reasoning, knowledge updates, and abstention.
The benchmark contains 500 curated questions embedded within freely scalable user-assistant chat histories.
LongMemEval presents a significant challenge to existing long-term memory systems, including commercial chat assistants.
The long-term memory capabilities of LLM-driven chat assistants in sustained interactions remain underexplored.
Long-context LLMs show a 30% accuracy drop on memorizing information across sustained interactions.
The paper presents a unified framework breaking down long-term memory design into three stages: indexing, retrieval, and reading.
Proposes memory design optimizations including session decomposition for value granularity, fact-augmented key expansion for indexing, and time-aware query expansion for refining search scope.
The proposed optimizations greatly improve both memory recall and downstream question answering on LongMemEval.
The study provides resources and guidance for advancing long-term memory capabilities of LLM-based chat assistants.
Limited progress in holistically evaluating memory capability in long-term interactions.
Existing benchmarks for long chat histories have shortcomings, including not accurately reflecting user-AI interactions.
Existing long-term memory benchmarks omit task-oriented dialogues, which are a significant portion of chat assistant usage and challenge memorization with long-context inputs and long-form responses.
Current benchmarks' interactive histories have non-configurable lengths of only a few thousand tokens, limiting difficulty as systems improve.
MemoryBank and PerLTQA insufficiently evaluate the ability to synthesize information across numerous sessions or reason with temporal metadata or time references.
All long-term memory benchmarks, including LoCoMo, fail to evaluate recall of information provided by the assistant or reasoning with updated user information.
LongMemEval is a comprehensive benchmark for assessing long-term memory capabilities of chat assistants, consisting of 500 manually created questions to test five core abilities.

LongMemEval is a benchmark for chat assistants on long-term interactive memory, covering five memory abilities: information extraction, multi-session reasoning, temporal reasoning, knowledge updates, and abstention.
The benchmark uses a pipeline inspired by the needle-in-a-haystack test to compile coherent and length-configurable chat histories for each question.
Two standard settings are provided: LongMemEvalS with approximately 115k tokens per problem and LongMemEvalM with 500 sessions (around 1.5 million tokens).
Long-context LLMs show a 30% to 60% performance drop on LongMemEvalS, indicating the benchmark's difficulty.
State-of-the-art commercial systems achieved only 30% to 70% accuracy in a setting much simpler than LongMemEvalS.
The paper presents a unified view for memory-augmented chat assistants, but the excerpt cuts off before detailing this view, leaving it as an incomplete future direction.

claims.interpretation: Round is a more optimal granularity than session for storing and utilizing interactive history, but further compression into individual user facts harms overall performance while improving multi-session reasoning accuracy.
Expanding flat index keys with extracted user facts improves memory recall by 9.4% and downstream question answering accuracy by 5.4% compared to using memory values as keys.
Naive time-agnostic memory designs perform poorly on temporal reasoning questions.

Proposes a simple indexing and query expansion strategy that explicitly associates timestamps with facts and narrows the search range, improving temporal reasoning memory recall by 6.8% to 11.3% when a strong LLM is used for query expansion.
Memory in LLM agents is under-evaluated due to lack of benchmarks.
The paper identifies four core competencies for memory agents: accurate retrieval, test-time learning, long-range understanding, and selective forgetting.
Existing benchmarks rely on limited context lengths or are tailored for static, long-context settings like book-based QA, which do not reflect the interactive, multi-turn nature of memory agents.
MemoryAgentBench is a new benchmark designed for memory agents, transforming existing long-context datasets and incorporating newly constructed datasets into a multi-turn format.
The benchmark simulates incremental information processing characteristic of memory agents and covers four core memory competencies.
Evaluation of diverse memory agents (from context-based and RAG systems to advanced agents with external memory) shows current methods fall short of mastering all four competencies.
The results underscore the need for further research into comprehensive memory mechanisms for LLM agents.
Existing agentic benchmarks focus on reasoning and leave memorization under-explored.
There is no unified benchmark for systematically evaluating memory quality in agents.
Recent memory-centric architectures employ diverse strategies for storing and retrieving past information.
This paper focuses on memory agents that use textual histories and external databases, as these are most common in real-world applications.
Memory encoded in model parameters is typically less capable than proprietary memory systems on closed-sourced API models.
The paper identifies four complementary competencies to evaluate memory agents, based on classic theories in memory and cognitive science.
One competency is Accurate Retrieval (AR), the ability to extract the correct snippet in response to a query, including one-hop or multi-hop retrieval.
Another competency is Test-Time Learning (TTL), the capacity to incorporate new behaviors or acquire new skills during deployment without additional training.
The paper defines four complementary competencies for memory agents: Long-Range Understanding (LRU), Selective Forgetting (SF), and two others (implied by context).
Early benchmarks (LOCOMO, LooGLE, LongBench) have relatively short contexts that no longer challenge current models.

claims.interpretation: Long-context benchmarks cannot be directly used to evaluate memory agents because they provide the entire context in a single block, whereas memory agents process context incrementally.

Memory is a compressed and distilled representation of past information, selectively extracting salient details and removing irrelevant information, unlike long context which stores all historical content verbatim.

Memory agents are designed to process context incrementally, absorbing input piece by piece, abstracting and consolidating information over time, generating new inferences, and learning novel rules from accumulated history.
LongMemEval (Wu et al., 2025) addresses the limitation of long-context benchmarks by using synthetic long-form conversations that can be injected into memory gradually, session by session.
